/MONDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
Issued at 147 PM CDT Sun Aug 30 2026

Heat:
Heat remains the main story of the foreseeable future. Not much
change from previous forecast cycles, with ensembles remaining 
in good agreement on the pattern through most of the week. 
Ridging aloft remains in place across the southeastern U.S., 
with a shortwave passing to the north of the Great Lakes region 
flattening the northern extent of the ridge midweek. The ridge 
builds back northwestward across the Central Plains behind the 
wave once it exits, perhaps getting a second a wind late in the 
week into next weekend. Even the AI global models/ensembles, 
which can sometimes be better at detecting the breakdown of 
persistent blocked highs like these at longer lead times, show 
no sign of true breakdown of the ridging through next weekend. 

Heat starts really settling in tomorrow, with expected highs in
the upper 90s to low 100s. Some wind gusts up to 25 mph are 
expected again tomorrow, especially late morning. The mixing 
associated with peak heating will help to reduce dew points and 
overall heat indices, but even with this drier air mass, it's 
going to feel quite hot. 1-2 degree differences in temperature
and/or dew point could result in us either overachieving our 
105 degree Heat Advisory criteria, or staying just below it, 
but a large portion of the area will be flirting with or meeting
criteria, so a Heat Advisory has been issued for 12 PM - 8 PM
Monday with impacts in mind. The warmest temperatures and heat
indices will be to the north and west of the plateau, with north
of I-44/along I-49 providing a reasonable proxy. 

Temperatures themselves don't necessarily increase as the week
continues, moreso remaining steadily in the upper 90s/low 100s,
but moisture does increase a bit as the week goes on, which does
lead to an increase in heat indices through the week. Perhaps
more notable is the lack of overnight relief, with nighttime
temperatures only falling to 75-80 degrees across much of the
area on Wednesday and Thursday. While repeated bouts of
afternoon mixing could help keep heat indices down during the
day and allow temperatures to fall lower at night in some areas,
the combination of 5+ days of highly anomalous heat and the 
likely record-high overnight lows (see Climate section below)
bring our HeatRisk well into the Major (Level 3 of 4) category
and into Extreme (Level 4 of 4) levels in northern/western
portions of the area every day this week. Right now, confidence
is quite high in 100+ degree heat indices through the remainder
of the week, but confidence is lower in the difference between 
105+ and 100-104 degrees for Tuesday and beyond. As such, an
Extreme Heat Watch has been issued beginning 12 PM on Tuesday
and continues through 8 PM Friday. This watch will be upgraded
a Heat Advisory and/or Extreme Heat Warning as confidence in
exact heat index values at individual locations becomes more
clear as the beginning of the week unfolds. 

Beyond the forecast period, CPC continues to highlight 60-70% 
chances of above normal temperatures continuing through 
September 13 in their 8-14 Day Outlook. 


Rain Chances (or lack thereof):
NBM rain chances remain <30% through the next 7 days. One thing
to consider with rainfall chances is that the shortwave to the
north of the Great Lakes may disrupt the pattern enough to
introduce low but mentionable PoPs Thursday and beyond,
especially if the westward retrograde of the ridge behind that
wave moves it far enough west to position us along its eastern
edge, which might allow us to get some "ridge rider" storms.
That being said, the most likely scenario progged by ensembles 
keeps us well under the influence of the ridge, and precip free,
for at least the next week. 

Drought/Fire Weather:
The combination of prolonged hot and dry conditions will
exacerbate the existing drought conditions, which have been in a
degrading trend over the last several weeks. CPC and WPC
continue to highlight rapid onset drought across the portions of
our area that don't already have D1 or D2 drought conditions
over the next 3-14 days. In addition to the obvious agricultural
impacts from drought, another component to monitor is the
potential early onset of the fall fire season as a result of 
early drying of fuels, especially fine fuels like grasses. 

Moisture does slowly increase through this week, but Monday and
Tuesday will see portions of our area reach minimum afternoon 
RHs between 25-35%. Be mindful of elevated fire weather concerns
potentially materializing earlier than normal with these
conditions this week.
